name: Practices for running an AI-first business, rated by strength of evidence
description: Management practices for building and running a business with AI, one row per practice. Each row gives a summary, the theme, the stage, the company sizes it fits, when to do it, the effort, the evidence level and flags, the studies for and against, and the company cases linked to it.
licence: Data: CC BY 4.0, Paweł Szczęsny, ai-first.company

rows.title: Map tasks before deciding what to automate
rows.summary: Break jobs into tasks and look at each one. Published scores rate how much of a job AI could do, its “exposure”. Treat a high score as a place to look, not as a decision to automate.

rows.title: Protect psychological safety during an AI rollout
rows.summary: AI projects can make staff afraid to speak up and unwilling to share what they know. Say early what AI means for jobs, and consult the people affected.

studies.citation: Kim, Kim and Lee (2025). The dark side of artificial intelligence adoption: linking artificial intelligence adoption to employee depression via psychological safety and ethical leadership. Humanities and Social Sciences Communications, 12(1).

rows.title: Budget for people and process, not just tools
rows.summary: Licences are the small part of the cost. Plan most of the time and money for training, redesigning work, and helping people through the change.

studies.citation: van Veen, Zhu and Ravesteyn (2026). How AI Implementation Barriers Shape AI Maturity? The Interacting Roles of Skilled Employees, Technological Infrastructure and Data Quality. CONF-IRM 2026 Proceedings, 17.

rows.title: Keep a person checking anything that goes to a customer or carries legal weight
rows.summary: Before AI output leaves the company or is relied on in a decision, a named person checks it against real sources and signs it off. Make the check a step in the process, with time allowed for it.

rows.title: Train staff on the tools you actually chose
rows.summary: Show every user what your chosen AI tool is, where it goes wrong, and what they must check. Use your own tasks and your own rules, give people time to practise, and include temporary staff.

studies.citation: Pinski, Adam and Benlian (2023). AI Knowledge: Improving AI Delegation through Human Enablement. Proceedings of the 2023 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems.

cases.company: Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (Victoria)
UK Department for Business and Trade

rows.title: Ask AI vendors for proof before you buy, and test on your own material
rows.summary: Do not take an AI vendor’s accuracy figure or “fully compliant” promise on trust. Ask how it was tested and on what, run a small test on your own material, and check the terms on your data and on leaving.

rows.title: Budget for the work AI creates
rows.summary: AI removes some work and adds other work: checking its output, keeping records, handling exceptions and looking after the tools. Count that work and give it an owner before you count the saving.

rows.title: Decide what data may go into which AI tools
rows.summary: Sort your data into two or three groups and say which AI tools each group may go into. Client secrets and personal data stay out of public tools. Where a mistake would be serious, block the upload instead of relying on a rule.

cases.company: Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (Victoria)

rows.title: Know the rules that already apply to your AI use
rows.summary: Most of the rules that bind your use of AI are not AI laws. You answer for what your AI says and does under the consumer, privacy, advertising and professional rules you already follow. List your AI uses and match each to its rules.

cases.company: Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (Victoria)

rows.title: Measure time saved per task against a baseline
rows.summary: Record how long a task takes and how good the result is before you add AI. Without that starting figure you cannot tell a real gain from a hopeful one.

studies.citation: Humlum and Vestergaard (2025). Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI. NBER Working Paper 33777 (revised March 2026).

cases.company: UK Department for Business and Trade

rows.title: Name one accountable AI owner
rows.summary: Give one named senior person the responsibility for AI: priorities, budget, risk and results. Shared responsibility tends to mean nobody decides.

studies.citation: McKinsey & Company (2025). The State of AI: Global Survey 2025. McKinsey Global Survey, published 5 November 2025.
Wojewodzic (2026). AI Transformation in Polish Organisations: The Gap Between Individual Adoption and Organisational Maturity. e-mentor, 2(114), 75–83.

rows.title: Start with one costly process, not a company-wide rollout
rows.summary: Pick one process that visibly costs time or money. Apply AI there, with a person checking the output, and expand only when the numbers move.

studies.citation: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (2025). Generative AI at Work. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 140(2), 889–942.
Humlum and Vestergaard (2025). Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI. NBER Working Paper 33777 (revised March 2026).

rows.title: Start with ready-made AI in software you already use, before building your own
rows.summary: Your office, accounting, support and sales software probably has AI features now. Try those on one task, with a few licences and a measured result, before you pay anyone to build something custom.

cases.company: UK Department for Business and Trade

rows.title: Write a one-page AI-use policy staff will actually read
rows.summary: Put the rules for AI on one page: which tools are allowed, what must never be typed in, who checks the output, and who to ask. Then build the most important rule into the work itself, because a page alone gets ignored.

cases.company: Department of Families, Fairness and Housing (Victoria)

rows.title: For each kind of task, test whether a person with AI beats either one alone
rows.summary: Do not assume that adding a person to AI, or AI to a person, gives the best result. Test it for each type of task before you settle the process.

rows.title: Do not treat a maturity score as a forecast
rows.summary: An AI maturity or readiness score describes where you say you stand. Evidence that a higher score leads to better results is thin and disputed. Use it to start a discussion, not to predict returns.

studies.citation: Thordsen and Bick (2023). A decade of digital maturity models: much ado about nothing?. Information Systems and e-Business Management, 21(4), 947–976.

rows.title: Give AI assistance to newer staff first
rows.summary: When you roll out an AI assistant for a well-defined task, start with your less experienced people. Studies find they gain the most.

studies.citation: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond (2025). Generative AI at Work. The Quarterly Journal of Economics, 140(2), 889–942.

rows.title: Make the AI show what its answer is based on
rows.summary: A score or an estimate with no reason attached is hard to judge. Choose and set up AI tools so that each answer comes with what it rests on: the marked part of the image, the similar past cases, the passage in the document.

studies.citation: Senoner, Schallmoser, Kratzwald, Feuerriegel and Netland (2024). Explainable AI improves task performance in human–AI collaboration. Scientific Reports, 14, 31150.

counter_studies.citation: Vaccaro, Almaatouq and Malone (2024). When combinations of humans and AI are useful: A systematic review and meta-analysis. Nature Human Behaviour, 8(12), 2293–2303.

rows.title: Test AI knowledge instead of asking staff to rate their own
rows.summary: People judge their own skills poorly. To find out what your staff know about AI, use a short knowledge test or a second opinion, not only a self-rating.

studies.citation: Lintner (2024). A systematic review of AI literacy scales. npj Science of Learning, 9, 50.

rows.title: Assess readiness from several sources, not one executive’s rating
rows.summary: A readiness check filled in by one senior person reflects that person’s view. Ask staff and managers as well, and compare the answers with what you can observe.

studies.citation: Silva, São Mamede and Santos (2024). A new proposed model to assess the digital organizational readiness to maximize the results of the digital transformation in SMEs. Journal of Innovation & Knowledge, 10(1), 100644.

rows.title: Claim only what your AI has been tested to do
rows.summary: If you tell customers that your product or service uses AI, or how well it works, hold the evidence before you say it. Regulators treat “AI-powered” and “98% accurate” as factual claims like any other.

rows.title: Measure readiness and resistance separately
rows.summary: Staff can be keen on AI and worried about it at once. Ask about the two separately. A single “readiness” score hides the worry.

studies.citation: Repovš, Drnovšek and Kaše (2019). Change Ready, Resistant, or Both? Exploring the Concepts of Individual Change Readiness and Resistance to Organizational Change. Economic and Business Review, 21(2).

Chang, Zhang, Cai and Guo (2024). Does AI-Driven Technostress Promote or Hinder Employees’ Artificial Intelligence Adoption Intention? A Moderated Mediation Model of Affective Reactions and Technical Self-Efficacy. Psychology Research and Behavior Management, 17, 413–427.
Caci, Nyantakyi, Blum, Sonpar, Schultes, Albers and Clack (2025). Organizational readiness for change: A systematic review of the healthcare literature. Implementation Research and Practice, 6.

rows.title: Put your own records in order before you ask AI to predict from them
rows.summary: An AI that estimates a price, a time or a next step learns from your past jobs and customers. Get those records complete, consistent and in one place first. In the cases here, that was most of the work.

rows.title: Redesign the workflow instead of adding a tool to it
rows.summary: Giving people an AI tool inside an unchanged process changes little. Decide again who does each step, in what order, and where a person checks.

studies.citation: McKinsey & Company (2025). The State of AI: Global Survey 2025. McKinsey Global Survey, published 5 November 2025.
Brynjolfsson, Mitchell and Rock (2018). What Can Machines Learn and What Does It Mean for Occupations and the Economy?. AEA Papers and Proceedings, 108, 43–47.
Humlum and Vestergaard (2025). Still Waters, Rapid Currents: Early Labor Market Transformation under Generative AI. NBER Working Paper 33777 (revised March 2026).

rows.title: When AI output goes wrong, correct it fast and in the open
rows.summary: Decide now what happens when an AI error gets out: who is told, who withdraws or corrects the work, and who checks how far the problem goes. In the documented cases, firms that owned up quickly were treated far better than firms that defended the error.

rows.title: Run two tracks: hand some tasks to AI, give experts AI help on others
rows.summary: Treat AI work as two programmes. One automates repeatable digital tasks whose results are easy to check. The other gives experts AI help on work that cannot be handed over. Judge each by its own measure.

rows.title: Set the limits before the tool acts
rows.summary: Before an AI tool sets a price, sends a message or takes a step for you, write down what it must never do, how far it may go, and what needs a person. Build those limits into the tool, then test inside them.

rows.title: Keep the entry-level tasks that newcomers learn on
rows.summary: Before you automate routine work, check whether it is how juniors learn the job. If it is, keep some of it for them, or replace the learning another way.
